newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE - HK police scrap royal emblem, keep bagpipes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - HK police scrap royal emblem, keep bagpipes.

text.p: Mist swirls from a mountaintop down to a sheltered glen. Drums rattle and a bagpipe band skirls out a battle song, "Scotland the Brave." Bayonets flash and boots crunch on a parade ground.
A barrel-chested, red-haired drill instructor bellows the usual morale-boosting encouragement at recruits: "Most of you people are half asleep!"
So, a proud Scottish regiment prepares to say farewell in the twilight of British colonial rule?
Actually no. The Hong Kong police are getting ready to welcome a new ruler, the People's Republic of China, replacing British royal insignia with Beijing's five-starred red emblem.
But the bagpipes stay, top officers vow, along with an immaculate British military tradition of "bull" -- spit-and-polish turnout on parade.
Visiting Chinese police chiefs like what they see, leaders here insist. Their verdict on the bagpipes is unknown.
This is the Hong Kong Police Training School, where a sign at the gate says: "Weather Index: Temperature 90C, Humidity 87 - Light Exercise."
It depends what you mean by light. While the band played a medley of Scottish tunes, hundreds of armed, uniformed recruits marched and drilled in precision for an hour in oven-like heat.
Then they went off to unarmed combat and physical training. All before lunch.
CHINESE LANGUAGE IS REQUIREMENT FOR RECRUITS
They're all Chinese except for three senior-ranked Britons, everyone wearing the green summer uniform adopted by colonial police for decades.

Tapping a shoe in unison with the bagpipes is a Scot from Edinburgh, School Commandant Stuart McDouall, a 47-year-old career policeman. A former schoolteacher in the Falkland Islands of the South Atlantic, he has a Chinese wife and two sons and plans to remain in the force, normally till 55.
"I play the pipes myself and I am president of the band," says McDouall, giving a personal stamp to the future of a unit widely popular in Hong Kong at public events.
Outside his offices are pictures of British royalty inspecting the force. Those days are nearly over.

McDouall apologises that he has no business card for visitors. "Everything is being changed," he says, meaning the British crown is set to vanish by July 1 when China takes over Hong Kong as a special, autonomous region.

His deputy is David Tullon, 50, while the third Briton who acts effectively as a sergeant-major, carrying a wooden stave, is ex-army officer Clive Howard, whose title is chief drill and musketry inspector.

The school, with a staff of 500, gives basic training to 1,000 recruits at a time for Hong Kong's 27,000-strong paramilitary force. Entrants are all Chinese -- you have to read and speak Chinese to be eligible and then 95 percent of applicants are rejected.
NEVER UNDER-ESTIMATE THE POWER OF A WOMAN
Many newcomers are women. Some look slight, comments a heavyweight Western male journalist.
"Well, be careful. Each of them can throw you to the ground in a second -- I guarantee," says McDouall.
The paramilitary force is more like an army than any traditional British police force and it is effective -- Hong Kong has crime problems, but is one of the world's safest cities.

"In the 1970s it was a badly-run, corrupt force," says McDouall. "But we have made wholesale changes. We are the cleanest police force in every way in Asia and we are among the most modern forces in the world."

About the future as part of China: "I am confident there will be no major changes in policing or conditions of service. I am not ready to retire. Nothing will change beyond my cap badge. I did take an oath to Queen Elizabeth but I also undertook to serve the people of Hong Kong."
He doubts Beijing will seek to control or interfere, but he adds: "We are not going to become tools of oppression. That would be repugnant to me and I would not stay in the force."

On the People's Liberation Army, which will keep up to 10,000 troops in the territory, he says: "We will work with them and exercise with them. But they will only ever be called out if there is a grave breakdown of social order that police cannot handle."
